806.title: Rebuild my church
806.hook: at San Damiano a crucifix tells Francis to rebuild; he starts with stones
806.howItsDone: The San Damiano cross is kept in the Basilica of Saint Clare in Assisi, and copies of it hang in Franciscan churches and homes; pilgrims pray before it and visit the restored church of San Damiano.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Francis: a man who crossed the lines unarmed. Your line was across the lines. Today we step back, before Damietta, to how he started.

A small church outside the walls of Assisi, and it's falling down. Cracked walls, a sagging roof, a priest too poor to fix any of it. Inside hangs a painted cross, Christ stretched on it with his eyes wide open. A young man, the son of a rich cloth merchant, comes in to pray, restless, unsure what his life is for. He kneels in front of that cross. And, the early lives of Francis say, the cross speaks. The church is San Damiano.
screen: `A CHURCH FALLING DOWN.` → `A PAINTED CROSS, EYES OPEN.` → `THE CROSS SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: Bonaventure, in his life of Francis, gives the voice from the cross like this: Francis, go and repair my house, which, as you see, is falling into ruin. Francis took it literally. The roof was falling in, so he would fix the roof. He sold cloth from his father's shop, and a horse, and brought the money to the priest. The priest, afraid of Francis's father, wouldn't take it, and Francis tossed it onto a windowsill as if it were dust. With no money to spend, he begged for building stones in the streets of Assisi, where everyone knew him as a merchant's son. Some people mocked him. He carried stones on his own back, set them with his own hands, and the little church stood again. He went on to repair other chapels the same way. Only later, Bonaventure writes, did Francis come to see that the words were mainly about the Church itself, the Church Christ bought with his own blood. Saint Paul says the same about people, writing to a quarreling congregation, in the Douay-Rheims: "you are God's building." The brothers who gathered around Francis would carry his way far beyond Assisi. But it started with a young man doing the job right in front of him, literally, one stone at a time.

segments.voice: Find one small broken thing in your life, a loose button, a squeaky hinge, a promise you let slide, one you could actually fix rather than the biggest. Picture the first stone: the needle, the screwdriver, the message. If you pray, hold the words from the cross: go and repair my house.
San Damiano. The crumbling church outside Assisi whose cross spoke to Francis, who repaired it stone by stone before understanding the words meant the whole Church. Today's word.
Your line: start with stones. Big repairs begin with something small. Day eight hundred six, done.

807.title: The first crib (Greccio, 1223)
807.hook: Francis sets up a manger with an ox and donkey so people can see
807.howItsDone: Catholic families and parishes set up a crib, or nativity scene, for Advent and Christmas; some wait until Christmas Eve to lay the figure of the child in the manger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, San Damiano, and a cross that asked Francis to repair a house. Your line was start with stones.

A bundle of hay. An ox. A donkey. A rough wooden feeding trough in a hillside village called Greccio, in the middle of a winter night. People climb up from the farms with candles and torches, and the woods fill with light and singing. In Celano's telling no one lays a baby in the straw. There's a manger, two animals breathing in the cold, and a small man in a patched habit, overflowing with joy. Francis of Assisi has asked a friend to build this.
screen: `HAY, AN OX, A DONKEY.` → `TORCHES ON A WINTER NIGHT.` → `AN EMPTY MANGER.`

segments.voice: Thomas of Celano, who wrote an early life of Francis, says Francis wanted to see with his own eyes how the child of Bethlehem had lain in a manger, the hardship of it, the ox and the ass standing by. He had heard the Christmas story all his life. He wanted the village to see it, not only hear it. The Gospel line he had in mind is Luke's, which in the Douay-Rheims reads: "and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." The animals aren't in Luke. They come from the prophet Isaiah: "The ox knoweth his owner, and the ass his master's crib." A beast, the prophet says, knows where its food comes from. Tradition placed those two beside the manger, and Francis put real ones there. A priest celebrated Mass right over the manger. Francis, who was a deacon and never a priest, sang the Gospel and preached, and Celano says he called Jesus the child of Bethlehem, saying the word Bethlehem so tenderly it sounded like a lamb's bleat. Celano adds that one man there saw a child lying in the manger as if asleep, and Francis seemed to wake him. Celano doesn't call Greccio the first of anything; first is the title tradition gave it later. What Greccio gave was a habit. Catholic homes and parishes still set out a crib in Advent, with an ox and a donkey nearby. A faith you can stand in front of, and see.

808.title: The wounds (La Verna, 1224)
808.hook: near the end of his life, Francis receives the marks of the wounds of Christ
808.howItsDone: Franciscans keep a feast of the Stigmata of Saint Francis, and Franciscan friars care for the sanctuary at La Verna, where pilgrims still come to pray at the place of the vision.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Greccio: a manger, an ox and a donkey. Your line was so they could see.

"I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus in my body." Saint Paul wrote that to the Galatians, near the end of his letter. In another letter he lists beatings and a stoning, and some readers take the marks to be those scars, earned on the road. Now carry that sentence up a wooded mountain in Tuscany called La Verna, where Francis has gone with a few brothers to fast and pray, away from everyone. He is ill and worn out. What happens on that mountain gives Paul's word a new life: stigmata.
screen: `I BEAR THE MARKS.` → `A MOUNTAIN CALLED LA VERNA.` → `A WORN-OUT MAN AT PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Thomas of Celano and Saint Bonaventure both tell it. While Francis prays, he sees a figure like a seraph, the angel of Isaiah's vision, with six wings, and between the wings a man fixed to a cross. Francis is torn between joy at the beauty of it and grief at the suffering, and he doesn't understand what he has seen. When the vision fades, the accounts say, the signs of nails appear in his hands and feet, and a wound opens in his side. Not paint, not a vision any more, but wounds he has to wrap. He didn't show them off. Celano says he hid them with great care, covering his hands, wearing something on his feet, and only a few close brothers knew while he lived. The marks were something given, and he guarded them like a secret between friends. The Church reads the stigmata not as a magic trick but as love made visible: Francis had spent years trying to follow Christ in poverty and humility, and his body, the tradition says, came to carry the shape of that love. Paul's word for the marks became the Church's word for this. Franciscans keep a feast of the stigmata of Saint Francis, and La Verna is still a place of prayer. Some readers take the accounts as a miracle exactly as told, and some ask what the brothers saw and how they described it. Either way, it's the story of a man marked by love.

809.title: Canticle of the Creatures (1225)
809.hook: tradition says he was nearly blind when he sang of brother sun, sister water, and at the end sister death
809.howItsDone: Franciscans sing and pray the Canticle of the Creatures, sometimes called the Canticle of Brother Sun, and its opening words gave the title to a papal letter on care for creation, Laudato si'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, La Verna, and wounds Francis hid with great care. Your line was marked by love.

Laudato si', mi' Signore. Four words in the old Italian of Umbria, the everyday speech of Assisi, not the Latin of the Church: praised be you, my Lord. Tradition says Francis made the song that starts with them near the end of his life, sick, his eyes in pain, unable to bear the light, lying in a small hut near San Damiano, where Clare and her sisters lived. A man who could barely look at the sun named it first among the creatures. And he wanted his brothers to sing it out loud as they went about. Its first creature: Brother Sun.
screen: `PRAISED BE YOU, MY LORD.` → `IN THE SPEECH OF ASSISI.` → `A SICK MAN SINGS OF THE SUN.`

segments.voice: The canticle walks through creation and names everything like a relative. Brother sun, who brings the day, beautiful and radiant. Sister moon and the stars, bright and precious. Brother wind, and air, and every kind of weather. Sister water, which the song calls useful, humble, precious and pure. Brother fire, who lights the night, playful and strong. And our sister, mother earth, who feeds us and brings out fruit and colored flowers and grass. Nothing in it is just a thing. Everything is kin. Tradition says a verse was added when the bishop and the mayor of Assisi were feuding: praise for those who forgive for love, and bear sickness and trouble in peace. The brothers sang it in front of both men, the story goes, and the quarrel ended. Near the very end comes a line that is hard to sing lightly: praised be you, my Lord, for our sister bodily death, from whom no one living can escape. Not an enemy. Not a thief in the night. A sister. Tradition says Francis added it when he knew he was dying, and asked his brothers to sing the canticle to him. The song sits beside the psalms the Church already sang: in the Douay-Rheims, Psalm 148 calls on sun and moon and stars, fire and hail, snow and ice, mountains and beasts, to praise the Lord. Francis took that old call and made it a family, right down to sister death.

810.title: Clare and the monstrance
810.hook: tradition says Clare held up the Eucharist when soldiers attacked her convent
810.howItsDone: In Catholic churches the consecrated host is placed in a monstrance for adoration and Benediction, and parishes hold hours of Eucharistic adoration when people come to pray before it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a song of Brother Sun and sister water. Your line was sister death.

A statue of Clare of Assisi: a woman in a plain habit, holding a gold sunburst on a stand, with a small round window at the center. It's a monstrance, the vessel used to show the consecrated host so people can see it and pray. She holds it up, toward something just out of the frame. Clare was the young woman from Assisi who followed Francis into poverty, and yesterday's song, tradition says, was made in a hut beside her house, San Damiano. So what is just out of the frame? An army.
screen: `A GOLD SUNBURST ON A STAND.` → `HELD UP TOWARD SOMETHING.` → `WHAT'S OUT OF THE FRAME?`

segments.voice: The early Life of Saint Clare tells it. Soldiers serving the emperor, at war in the valley, came to San Damiano, climbed over the walls and got into the cloister. The terrified sisters ran to Clare. She was sick and could not walk. She had herself carried to the door, had the Body of the Lord brought and set in front of her, and lay down before it in prayer. With the words of a psalm, she asked God not to hand over to beasts the souls that confess to him, and to guard her sisters. The Life says she heard a voice, like a little child's, promising to protect them always. She asked for the city too, and was told it would suffer but be defended. She turned to the sisters and told them not to be afraid. The soldiers, the story says, scrambled back over the walls and left. And the vessel? The Life doesn't mention a gold monstrance. It speaks of a small box of silver and ivory, where the host was kept. The great sunburst belongs to the statues, not to the Life: true to the story's heart, if not to its silverware. Clare didn't wave a weapon or make a speech. She put the Eucharist between her sisters and the danger, and she held it up. The Douay-Rheims psalm puts the idea plainly: "Unless the Lord keep the city, he watcheth in vain that keepeth it."

811.title: Dominic (1170–1221)
811.hook: a Spanish canon starts an order of preachers who live poor and study hard
811.howItsDone: Dominican friars and sisters, and lay Dominicans, live a rhythm of prayer, study and preaching, and Dominican friars write O.P. after their names for the Order of Preachers.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare at the door of San Damiano, with soldiers on the wall. Your line was she held it up.

A student in a Spanish town is selling his books. In his day a book was handwritten on parchment, slow and costly, and these carry his own notes in the margins. But there's a famine, and people in the streets are starving. Jordan of Saxony, who knew him and wrote an early account of him, says he sold the books and gave the money away. A brother remembered him saying he would not study on dead skins while living people died of hunger. Years later, the same man would found an order built around study. His name was Dominic.
screen: `A STUDENT SELLS HIS BOOKS.` → `NOT ON DEAD SKINS.` → `THE SAME MAN BUILDS ON STUDY.`

segments.voice: Dominic became a canon, a priest living in community at the cathedral of Osma, and traveled north with his bishop, Diego. In the south of France they found preachers arriving with horses and servants and fine clothes, and being ignored. People there were listening to wandering teachers who lived poor. Diego and Dominic, Jordan says, drew a plain conclusion: if you want to be heard, go on foot, with nothing, the way the apostles went. Dominic gathered a small band of preachers, and the Church approved them as a new kind of religious order: not monks staying in one monastery, but friars sent out. They begged for their food, owned little, and went where people were. Jesus's charge at the end of Mark, in the Douay-Rheims, was their whole job description: "Go ye into the whole world, and preach the gospel to every creature." Then the books came back. A preacher needs something true to say, so Dominic sent his brothers to study, and study hard, in towns where the schools were. The student who sold his books for the hungry now asked his brothers to fill their heads, so they could feed people another way. Thomas Aquinas, a Dominican himself, later wrote that it is a greater thing to contemplate and pass on to others what you've contemplated than only to contemplate. Dominicans took that as their own, and still sign their names with the letters O.P., for the Order of Preachers. Prayer, then study, then the handing on.
screen: `PREACHERS ON HORSEBACK, IGNORED.` · `FRIARS ON FOOT, WITH NOTHING.` · `SENT TO STUDY, AND STUDY HARD.` · `CONTEMPLATE, THEN PASS IT ON.` · then, large: `PREACH THE GOSPEL TO EVERY CREATURE.`

812.title: The universities
812.hook: Paris grew from its cathedral school; Oxford and Bologna rose in the same age
812.howItsDone: Catholic universities today, and the Church's own pontifical faculties, keep the medieval pairing of faith and study; Catholics speak of theology as faith seeking understanding.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Dominic, who sold his books for the hungry and then sent his friars to study. Your line was to contemplate and to share.

An open book on a coat of arms, the arms of the University of Oxford, and written across its pages, Dominus illuminatio mea. The words open a psalm, in the Douay-Rheims: "The Lord is my light and my salvation, whom shall I fear?" A place famous for lectures and libraries and examinations chose, for its badge, a line of prayer. It's a clue to where the whole idea of a university came from.
screen: `DOMINUS ILLUMINATIO MEA.` → `A PSALM ON AN OPEN BOOK.` → `A CLUE TO WHERE IT CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: In the middle ages, bishops kept schools at their cathedrals to train clergy to read, to sing the liturgy and to understand scripture. In Paris, the school by the cathedral of Notre-Dame drew teachers, and the teachers drew students, until the streets around were full of both. In the cities, bakers and masons banded together into guilds to protect their trade. Teachers and students did the same. In Latin, such a sworn body could be called a universitas, a whole company of people bound together. The masters of Paris, the students of Bologna and the scholars of Oxford organized this way, and won rights from popes and kings to govern themselves. A day there was built on two things. The lecture: a master read a text aloud, line by line, and explained it. And the disputation: a question was posed, the arguments against were stated fairly, then the master gave his answer and replied to each objection. Some readers see Anselm's phrase from day eight hundred, faith seeking understanding, turned here into a daily routine. You didn't win by shouting. You had to state the other side fairly before you answered it. Degrees, the lecture hall, the idea that a question deserves an argument: these grew in schools where theology was taught alongside law and medicine and the arts. The friars from yesterday's story went to these towns to study and teach. Learning was treated as a way of loving God with the mind.
screen: `THE SCHOOL BY THE CATHEDRAL.` · `A GUILD OF MASTERS AND STUDENTS.` · `LECTURE, THEN DISPUTATION.` · `FAITH SEEKING UNDERSTANDING.` · then, large: `THE LORD IS MY LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Pick a hard question you've been avoiding, in your faith, your work or your life, and do what a disputation does: state the strongest case against your own view as fairly as you can, then let your answer come and see whether it meets the objection. There's no need to finish. If you pray, begin with the psalm's line, the Lord is my light.
University. The universitas: a sworn company of masters and students, growing in cities like Paris from the schools beside the cathedrals. Today's word.
Your line: faith builds schools. The week ran from the stones of San Damiano to the lecture hall. That's day eight hundred twelve.
